results.summary: This design drives a seven-segment display from eight input switches. It uses logic gates to map the switch states to the display segments, allowing the user to toggle the switches to turn on individual segments. Testing is done by turning on the switches and observing the display. It requires an external seven-segment display and switches.

This chip demonstrates various logic gates, including NOT, OR, NOR, XOR, AND, and NAND. The inputs are routed through these gates to produce outputs that reflect the gate operations. It can be tested by applying input signals and observing the outputs, optionally using a seven-segment display or LEDs for verification. The design is intended as an educational demonstration.

This design compares the behavior of OR versus XOR gates and AND versus NAND gates. Inputs 0 and 1 are fed to OR and XOR gates, while inputs 2 and 3 are fed to AND and NAND gates. The outputs can be observed with a seven-segment display or other indicators. The project is educational, highlighting the similarities and differences between these gate types.

This project allows the user to turn switches on or off to control LEDs. It uses logic gates to drive the LEDs based on the switch states. The design is simple and can be tested by toggling switches and observing the corresponding lights. External hardware includes LEDs and switches.

This is an 8-to-3 encoder that uses logic gates to display characters on a seven-segment display. For example, when inputs 1-5 are on, the display shows the letter 'F'. It can be tested by setting the inputs and observing the display. No external hardware is required beyond the seven-segment display.

This is a 2-bit adder that takes two inputs (A and B) and produces sum and carry outputs. Inputs 0 and 1 represent A and B; the sum is output on OUT0 and the carry on OUT1. It can be tested by applying input combinations and verifying the outputs against expected addition results. An external PMOD LED display can be used to visualize the outputs.

This design uses seven input pins and provides seven output pins to drive a seven-segment display. The specific logic implemented is not described, so its exact function is unclear. It can be tested by connecting the outputs to a seven-segment display. External hardware required is a seven-segment display.

This chip contains a secret code that activates a 'lock' when entered correctly, indicated by a light. The code is entered via the input pins, and the output pins drive a seven-segment display and an LED. Testing involves troubleshooting to discover the correct code. External hardware includes a seven-segment display and an LED.

This design lights up segments of a seven-segment display to form the letter 'b' with a period at the end. The segments are controlled by switches: switches 1 and 2 control the bottom-right segment (OR logic), switches 3 and 4 control the bottom segment (AND logic), and switches 5-8 control other segments individually. It can be tested by toggling switches and observing the display. External hardware includes an LED display and switches.

This is a half adder that adds two input bits and produces sum and carry outputs. Inputs IN0 and IN1 are the two bits, with the sum on OUT0 and carry on OUT1. It can be tested by applying all four input combinations and verifying the outputs. No external hardware is specified beyond the chip itself.
